How does a language model represent numbers? Or does one representation contain many things at once, magnitude, digit identity, position, parity etc.?

Model · Qwen3.5-4B
TL;DR

The question was whether a language model holds a number as one unified concept, or as a bundle of simultaneously-encoded properties, magnitude, digit identity, digit position, parity, and so on, and whether those properties live in separate, readable directions.

After seven experiments, the evidence points clearly to a multiplexed representation:

The model builds a complete, linearly-decodable representation of every numerical property by the very first layer (L0), magnitude, all three digits, parity, digit count, digit sum, and it stays decodable (≈1.0) through all 32 layers, at both the number's token and the end of the sentence. Those properties sit in near-orthogonal linear directions (magnitude is ~86–90° from each digit-identity direction from L0 onward), and each remains fully decodable after the others are linearly removed. The encoding is essentially linear, a small MLP never beats the linear probe.

Magnitude shows a mildly logarithmic geometry, though partly confounded by digit count. Digits are not circular. The same digit is represented similarly across positions. The early-layer code is context-stable (a probe trained in one sentence transfers to another) before becoming context-specific in mid-layers. The model does not converge 54, 6 × 9, 108 / 2 into a shared abstract code. And the early-layer representations are causally effective: patching 54→64 shifts only magnitude, leaving parity and the units digit intact.

So a number is not "one concept". It's closer to a set of parallel, linear, mostly-independent features, assembled in layer 0, and still readable (and causally usable) for the rest of the network.

I started thinking about this question while reading about linear representations [1]The Linear Representation Hypothesis is the idea that high-level, abstract concepts (like gender, tense, or language) are encoded as linear directions or subspaces inside the high-dimensional internal spaces of neural networks and language models in language models. I wondered if that worked for words, would it work for numbers, coz they are inherently tricky to represent? You can represent most words using a single vector that represents their semantic meaning, but for digits, its tricky. For example, is the number 54 a single concept, or a combination of its magnitude, its digits, and their positions? And how does that relate to 6 × 9, which has the same value but a completely different form? Are they represented as a graph, with 6 and 9 somehow "connected" to 54?

This blog is a dump of all the findings from my experiments trying to answer these questions. I picked two concrete hypotheses to test, Levy and Geva [2] report a circular, per-digit, base-10 structure in the models and tasks they studied, and AlquBoj et. al. [3] report sub-linear, logarithmic-like spacing for numerical magnitude. I treated both as hypotheses about my model, Qwen3.5-4B, rather than given facts, and let the data decide.

I have organized this work so that each experiment answers one question: 0, how numbers are tokenized (for this model); 1, which properties can be decoded and from which layer; 2, the geometry of those readouts (logarithmic? circular? positional?); 3, whether magnitude, digits, and parity are independently recoverable; 4, whether the representation is stable across sentence context; 5, whether different expression formats converge; and 6, whether the early-layer states are causally used.

§

Before the experiments: how I'm measuring anything

A transformer is, at its core, a long residual stream: a vector that flows from the input embeddings to the output, with every layer (mlp and attention) adding a little to it. To see "how the model represents a number," I read the stream. I feed the model a fixed sentence, "The number is 54.", and I capture the residual vector at every layer (the input embedding, then the output of each of the 32 blocks).

I capture it at hl>:

Number-token position. The residual at the last digit of the number. So for e.g., for a number like 871, we take the token embedding of the digit 1 as it is the last.

Sentence-final position. The residual at the final token (.). This includes whatever the model does with the number after reading it, that is, the context of the number and the sentence.

To decide what a property like "the value is 54" means for the model, I used a standard linear probe: fit a small linear function on top of a frozen layer's activations to predict a property (value, units digit, parity, …). If a single linear function can read it out, the information is stored in a linear, geometrically meaningful way, a direction in the vector space. I lean on linear probes heavily throughout this project and only bring in a small neural net as a contrast (in experiment 3).

The single most important discipline, though, was splitting the data by number, not by sentence. If I randomly mixed prompts, a probe could just memorize "54 looks like this," and I'd be fooled. So I always hold out entire values, train on some numbers, test on numbers it has never seen, plus separate splits for unseen digit combinations and unseen magnitudes.

How the probes are actually scored ›
  • Continuous properties (value, log-value, digit sum) are regressed and scored by held-out R². 1.0 = perfect, 0 = no better than guessing the mean.
  • Categorical properties (units/tens/hundreds digit, digit count, parity) are classified and scored by balanced accuracy, the average per-class accuracy, so a probe that just always says "even" can't win. 0.5 = chance for two classes.
  • Probes are fit with a small L2 penalty and a fixed random seed, and I report held-out performance only.
  • All numbers are integers 0–999. I read the last digit token of the number (tokens 0–9 map to IDs 15–24 in this model).
0

How are the numbers tokenized?

This preliminary experiment establishes how numerical strings enter the model. Before I extract the activations, I need to know how the tokenizer splits up numbers, because that determines how much "compositional" work the network even has to do. If 54 is one token, its embedding could already carry the whole value. If it's split into 5 and 4, the model gets to build the number from parts in its layers.

For Qwen3.5-4B integers are tokenized digit-by-digit. There is no whole-number token for 54 or 154; the vocabulary has individual digit tokens, and every integer is a sequence of them.

So the same digit has the same ID whether it's the units, tens, or hundreds place. So the model's input is already digit-identity, the positional value of a digit is something the layers must add on top, and that's a question I'll return to in experiment 2.

Alternate forms break the clean pattern, fifty-four and 5.4e1 tokenize into multiple, irregular chunks. I keep that in mind for experiment 5, where I ask whether all these spellings of the same value ever converge.

Fig 1 Tokenization audit (0–999). Every integer is split into exactly as many tokens as it has digits, and each digit maps to its own fixed ID (15–24). No whole-number tokens exist in the vocabulary.

1

What can we decode, and from which layer?

Now the real question. For every layer, I train a separate linear probe to read out each property of the number: the value, the log of the value, the units, tens and hundreds digits, the digit count, the parity Here, the parity refers to the parity of the number as a whole, not the individual digits., and the digit sum. I do this at both the number-token position and the sentence-final position. The question I'm asking of the plot is: does understanding build up gradually as we go deeper?

Key finding. Every single property is already decodable to ≈1.0 in layer 0, the first block, and it stays there, flat, all the way to the final layer. Magnitude (R²≈0.996), all three digits (balanced accuracy ≈1.0), parity (≈1.0), digit count, digit sum. The only thing that's "not there" is the input embedding itself, which is just the raw token and naturally can't yet hold the composed value.

In other words, the model does not gradually learn what a number is as it goes deeper. It assembles a full, clean, linear number representation in one step, at the very top of the stack, and then simply maintains it.

Fig 2 Probes at the number-token position. All properties jump to near-perfect at L0 and hold.

Fig 3 Generalization controls. The strong performance survives splits by unseen values, unseen digit combinations, and unseen magnitudes, it's not memorization.

The generalization panel is the one I'd point to if you only looked at one chart. A probe that reaches ~1.0 on values it has never seen, and on digit combinations and magnitudes it has never seen, is doing real composition, not recall. And the same flat, near-perfect profile appears at the end of the sentence, so this isn't an artifact of reading the token right after it was written.

One property deserves a footnote: log(n) is the hardest continuous target. That's expected and partly definitional, log(0) is undefined, so I model it as log(1+n). The linear value probe is the clean magnitude readout and it's essentially perfect from L0.

2

The geometry of the number code

Knowing that a property is decodable doesn't tell me how it's arranged. So I test the three concrete geometric ideas: is magnitude spaced logarithmically? Are individual digits laid out on a circle? Is a digit's identity separable from its position? I do these as separate sub-experiments, each with its own null hypothesis.

2.1  Is magnitude logarithmic?

The logarithmic hypothesis says the model cares about relative differences: that 5→6 is a "bigger" step than 50→51. If true, the distance between two numbers' activations should track |log a − log b| better than |a − b| This is my assumption; contact me and let me know if you don't agree with this.. I compute the full pairwise activation distance matrix (cosine and Euclidean, separately), build the corresponding linear and log theoretical matrices, and take the Spearman correlation, at every layer.

interactiveDoes distance track linear or log value?

Moderate, with a confound. The log model does correlate better with activation distance than the linear model (at the final layer ≈0.47 vs ≈0.26), and the fitted power exponent is small (β≈0.05–0.09), consistent with a gently sub-linear spacing. So there is a mild logarithmic flavor.

But I would not call this a clean "log code." Digit count is strongly confounded with magnitude here (a 3-digit number is always bigger than a 2-digit one), and the same digit-count effect produces an apparent log correlation. The conclusion: mildly log-like, partly digit-count-driven.

2.2  Are digits circular?

The circular hypothesis (the one from Levy & Geva's work) is: digit d sits at angle 2πd/10 on a circle, so that 0 is neighbors with 9. If the model did this, the similarity between digit i and j should follow cos(2π(i−j)/10). I test it by fitting the circular model and scoring it against alternatives (a linear model and a quadratic model) on held-out digits and contexts.

interactiveCircular model vs alternatives, per layer
The tell-tale: if 0 wraps to 9, then sim(0,9) should exceed sim(0,5). At a layer of your choosing;
L8

Null result. The circular model does not beat a simple quadratic model at any layer (r²_circ ≈0.31–0.34 vs r²_quad ≈0.34–0.39), and the wrap-around signature is absent: sim(0,9) is not more similar than sim(0,5). Whatever structure the model has for a digit, it isn't the 10-point circle.

2.3  Is a digit's identity separate from its position?

We know 54 = 5×10 + 4. The digit 5 contributes 50 here, 500 in 500, and 5 in 505. The model's input tokens are position-blind (a 5 is always token ID 20). So the interesting question: does the model keep a stable identity for the digit 5, and add position as a separate feature? I check whether the same digit, sitting in different positions, lands in similar activations, versus different digits.

interactiveSame digit across positions vs different digits

Key finding. The same digit in different positions stays highly similar (≈0.9 across layers), while different digits stay far apart (≈ −0.1). If you remember from our first experiment, we can infer the digit positions from early-layer activations. Now we see that the same digit similarity also doesn't change much in any layer. This points to a position-invariant digit identity: the model does keep a stable "this is the digit 5" signal and treats its positional value as a separate, addable feature.

Fig 4 Magnitude geometry. Cosine/Euclidean distance vs linear and log value across layers, plus the fitted power exponent β.

3

Are these properties independent?

Here's the trap. I've shown I can decode magnitude, digits, and parity. But "I can read all of them out" does not mean the model stores them separately. They could all be smeared into one shared representation. To find out whether the properties are genuinely independent, I run three complementary tests.

3.1  Do they live in different directions?

I extract the linear probe direction for each property and measure the angle between them. If magnitude and digit identity used the same directions, the angle would be near 0°. If they're separate, it should be near 90°. The plot compares the embedding with the output of the first transformer block.

interactiveThe angle between "magnitude" and "the digit", as it opens up
L0
Magnitude, the value direction (fixed).
Units digit, rotated by the measured angle.

Key finding. In the raw input embedding, the magnitude and digit directions are nearly collinear (≈1.8°), which makes sense: the input is just digits, and value is a function of them. Then, in layer 0, the angle snaps open to ≈86° and holds near-orthogonal for the rest of the network. The model's first act is to un-mix magnitude from digit identity into separate, perpendicular directions. That's a single, clean, early "decomposition" event.

3.2  Can I remove one and still read the others?

Angles are suggestive but not proof, correlated quantities can have orthogonal decoders. The sharper test is residualization: I linearly remove the component of the activation that predicts magnitude, then ask whether digit identity is still decodable. Then I flip it, remove digit info and ask whether magnitude survives. If both survive, the information is genuinely separable, not just decorrelated.

interactiveDecodability after removing the other property

Key finding. Digits remain ≈1.0 decodable even with magnitude linearly removed, and magnitude stays ≈0.99 with digits removed. The information is independently recoverable in both directions. (Caveat, as always: linear residualization can't remove a nonlinear dependency, which is exactly what the next test checks.)

3.3  Is a nonlinearity hiding in here?

The final independence test: for each property, I train both a linear probe and a small MLP (matched, strictly held-out, so the net can't just memorize numbers) and compare. If the information were tucked into a nonlinear arrangement, the MLP would win.

interactiveMLP minus linear (per property, all layers)

Null result, and a good one. The MLP never beats the linear probe for any property at any layer (the difference is ≤0 everywhere). So there is no nonlinear "bonus" to be had, the numerical properties are stored in a way that is linearly accessible. This is the cleanest possible answer to "is it a messy nonlinear representation?": no, it's linear.

Fig 5 Independence of numerical properties. Inter-direction angles open from ~2° (embedding) to ~86° (L0+); residualization leaves each property decodable; the MLP adds nothing over linear.

4

Does the representation change with context?

Up to here, every number lived in one fixed sentence: "The number is 54." But in the wild, 54 shows up as a quantity, an arithmetic answer, a divisor, a year, a temperature. I take the same numbers and drop them into six different sentence frames, keeping the number constant and only changing the surrounding words. Then I ask: does a probe trained in one frame still work in another?

interactiveCross-context probe transfer (trained on "neutral", tested per context)

Key finding, with a twist. Magnitude is context-stable. A value probe trained on the neutral frame transfers to every context at ≈0.99, across all layers. The model's "how big is this number" signal is robust to the surrounding sentence.

The twist is in the finer properties. Units-digit and parity transfer well in the early layers but degrade in the mid-to-late layers when the context is arithmetic or divisibility, where the surrounding words are doing real numerical work and start to compete with the bare digit. So: the core magnitude is stable everywhere; the digit-level detail is stable early and gets context-specific later.

Fig 6 Context stability. Cross-context similarity of the same number, and probe transfer across the six sentence frames. Magnitude is stable throughout; units/parity transfer well early, then become context-specific.

5

Do different formats converge on one number?

Here's my favorite question, and the most ambitious: does the model build an abstract "value" that is independent of how the number was spelled? Consider that 54, 50 + 4, 6 × 9, and 108 / 2 all name the same quantity. If the model had a real abstract number, these four inputs should converge toward the same activation as it works. I test two ways: (1) do equivalent expressions become more similar to each other across layers? and (2) can a probe trained on plain integers recover the value from an arithmetic expression?

interactiveEquivalent expressions vs a within-format baseline

Null result. Equivalent expressions do not converge. Within a single format, different values are strongly separated (high, near-perfect R²), good. But across formats, a probe trained on plain integers fails to recover the value from an arithmetic expression (R² ≈ 0, and the "convergence" of equivalent expressions is at or below the random-pair baseline). The model is not building a shared, format-invariant number here.

Two honest caveats. First, I can't fully rule out that the model does compute the value but in a frame that my integer-trained probe can't read (the "Calculate the result:" prompt changes the task). Second, near the end of the prompt the model is about to generate the same answer token, which can pull representations together for output reasons, so I read the mid-expression layers as the truer signal, and there's no convergence there either. Bottom line: no evidence of a unified abstract numerical code in this 4B model.

Fig 7 Equivalent expressions. Within-format value separation is strong; cross-format transfer and expression convergence are at/below baseline, no shared abstract number.

6

Causal test: do these representations actually do anything?

I've established that magnitude, digits, and parity are all decodable. But decodable ≠ causally used. A feature could be readable without the model ever relying on it. To close the loop, I do activation patching: I take the base sentence "The number is 54.", and at a chosen layer I replace its activation with the one from "… is 64." or "… is 75.", then see which of the model's behaviors change. I also patch in a random activation as the control. If a direction is genuinely functional, the targeted patch should shift exactly the property I expect, and the random patch should do nothing.

The two targets are chosen to be different: 64 differs from 54 only in the tens digit (so magnitude changes, parity and the units digit stay put), while 75 changes both tens and units (so magnitude, parity, and units all should move).

interactiveWhat does a patch actually change?
PropertyBase (54)After patch (64)Random control
Green = the property changed after the patch. Gray = unchanged. The random column should always stay gray, if it doesn't, the effect isn't specific to the number.

Key finding, the payoff. Patching 54→64 at the early layers (L4, L8) shifts magnitude (5→6) while leaving parity (still even) and the units digit (still 4) exactly intact. Patching 54→75 shifts all three. And the random control shifts nothing. That's exactly the dissociation I was hoping for: I can move the model's "how big" readout independently of its "which digits" readout. The early-layer number code isn't just readable, the model uses it, and its parts are separable.

The tested effect is absent at L24 and L31. This experiment does not determine why patching at later layers differs.

Fig 8 Causal validation. Patching 54→64 moves magnitude only; 54→75 moves all properties; random patches move nothing. The effect is strongest in the early layers.

Stay humble. A difference vector like h₆₄ − h₅₄ is not a clean feature intervention by itself, it can carry a lot of incidental change. The fact that I see a selective effect (magnitude moves, digits don't) and a null random control is strong evidence, but the fully rigorous version would use a validated magnitude subspace with norm-matched and random-subspace controls. I'd treat this as compelling, not conclusive, causal support.

★

So what is a number, to this model?

I set out with three candidate stories: a unified number, a multiplexed one, or a distributed/nonlinear one. The results are most consistent with the multiplexed account under these measurements. Let me lay out the verdict on each hypothesis, with the evidence that decided it:

Supported · strong

Multiplexed, linear, near-orthogonal

Magnitude, digits, and parity are simultaneously present from L0, linearly decodable (MLP adds nothing), in ~86°-separated directions, independently recoverable, context-stable, and causally effective. This is the model.

Rejected

Circular digit code

The circular model doesn't beat a quadratic model, and the 0≈9 wrap-around is absent. The tested digit similarities do not show the predicted wrap-around. r²_circ ≤ r²_quad everywhere

Partly

Logarithmic magnitude

Log value correlates better than linear value (β≈0.05–0.09), so there's a mild log flavor, but it's substantially confounded by digit count. Real, but weaker than the headline suggests.

Supported

Position-invariant digits

The same digit stays similar across positions (≈0.9) while different digits don't (≈−0.1). Identity and positional value are separate, composable features.

Rejected

Format-invariant abstraction

54, 6×9, 108/2 do not converge, and an integer-trained probe can't read the value out of an arithmetic expression. No shared abstract number.

Rejected

Nonlinear / distributed

The "messy blob" story loses to the linear one at every layer for every property. If there's nonlinearity, it buys the probes nothing.

The picture that falls out of all seven experiments: the model builds a clean, linear, multiplexed number in layer 0, magnitude, digits, and parity as near-orthogonal, independently-readable, causally-used features, and then carries that tidy code, largely unchanged, through the rest of the network.

This interpretation provides a useful starting point for further experiments. It means small-integer reasoning in a small LLM isn't some opaque, nonlinear process, it's a set of inspectable directions you can read, and even steer. Further work can test whether these readouts are useful targets for controlled interventions. And it sharpens where the hard part actually is: not representing a number, but combining numbers across different formats, the abstraction that this model, at least, doesn't seem to have built.

Where I'd be careful / what's next

Three honest limits. (1) Scope: integers 0–999 in one model (a 4B), the log and abstraction results could shift with larger numbers, real decimals, or a bigger model. (2) Confounds: the log-magnitude signal is digit-count-confounded, and the cross-format test conflates format with task frame. (3) Causality: the patching is suggestive but not the subspace-controlled gold standard. The natural next steps: a proper norm-matched causal study, a real abstract-arithmetic task (where the model must compute, not just recognize), and testing whether the "early, linear, orthogonal" structure is a general property or specific to small integers.

Parity generally means the state of being equal, balanced, or equivalent in value, rank, amount, or status.
